To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the chromosome 3B is highly variable at the gene and TE levels among the accessions of the Triticeae diversity collection, and that the variability is particularly high at the chromosome extremities, suggesting that these regions may be involved in genome evolution.

(i) 23% of genes on chromosome 3B of wheat are variable in a Triticea diversity panel of 44 accessions; (ii) 60% of TE-derived reference markers are absent in at least on accession, revealing a level of variability in TE space higher than that observed in genes; and (iii) chromosome extremities are the region where most of the variability is located.

(1) 330 genes are absent from the reference genome, (2) 23% of all genes are variable within the panel, (3) 60% of TE markers are absent in at least an accession, (4) chromosome extremities are the genomic regions where we observed the most variability, and (5) our results suggest a phylogeny of the Triticeae with independent hybridization event leading to different hexalploid species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of structural variations affecting genes and transposons in wheat, a species of major agronomical interest, and provides insights into the evolution of the complex Triticeaea genomes.
the study of SVs in a Triticea diversity panel, and it has led to the identification of a large number of genes and TEs that are absent from the reference genome.
the study of structural variations affecting genes and transposons in a diversity panel of wheat and related species, which will help us to understand the origin and evolution of wheat genomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Triticeae genomes have evolved by a complex process involving a combination of chromosomal duplications, deletions, translocations, and inversions.
the genome of wheat is highly variable and that the wheat genome has evolved through a complex process of chromosomal rearrangements and gene and TE loss.
the genome of wheat is highly variable and that the reference genome is not a true reference.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Triticeae genomes are highly dynamic at the intraspecies and interspecies levels, and that the wheat genome has undergone multiple rearrangements and gene losses.
we have identified a high level of SVs affecting the wheat genome and that these variations are likely to impact the phenotypic diversity of the crop.

SVs affecting genes are common in Triticeae and are mostly due to presence/absence variations of genes, and SVs affecting TEs are also common and are mostly due, at the intraspecies level, to copy number variation of TEs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a better understanding of the genome structure of wild and cultivated accessions will be crucial to improve the use of wheat as a crop.
the use of high-coverage sequencing of sorted chromosomes is a powerful approach to assess the extent of SV in polyploid crops and to provide new insights into their evolution.
SVs are widespread in the Triticeae genomes, which is a major factor that should be considered in future studies aiming to unravel the complex genetic basis of phenotypic variations in these crops.
